title: Chronic kidney disease
blurb: Classify CKD by eGFR and ACR, set the right blood pressure target, monitor ACE inhibitors safely, and know when to refer, using NICE NG203.
question: Mrs Adeyemi, 66, has type 2 diabetes. Her eGFR has been 48 for 6 months and her urine ACR is 82 mg/mmol. What clinic blood pressure should she aim for?

teach.body: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) means abnormal kidney structure or function present for 3 months or more: an eGFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m², and/or markers of kidney damage such as an albumin:creatinine ratio (ACR) of 3 mg/mmol or more. It is classified on two axes: filtration (G1–G5) and albuminuria (A1–A3). Plain English: how well the kidneys filter, and how much protein is leaking, together predict risk.

teach.caption: eGFR in mL/min/1.73 m², ACR in mg/mmol. Risk of adverse outcomes rises with lower eGFR and higher ACR. G1 is 90+ and G2 60–89 (CKD only with damage markers).

items: Avoid meat for 12 hours before an eGFR blood test, and get the sample to the lab within 12 hours.
Confirm a first eGFR below 60 by repeating it within 2 weeks.
Use urine ACR, not PCR, to detect proteinuria in adults.
Confirm an ACR of 3–70 mg/mmol on an early morning sample; 70 or more needs no repeat.

teach.caption: These are clinic readings. More protein leak means a tighter target.

teach.h: ACE inhibitors, ARBs and SGLT-2 inhibitors
teach.body: Offer an ACE inhibitor or ARB (titrated to the highest tolerated dose) to adults with CKD and diabetes if ACR is 3 or more; with hypertension if ACR is above 30; and without diabetes if ACR is 70 or more (with nephrology referral). Never combine two renin–angiotensin antagonists. SGLT-2 inhibitors are added to optimised ACE inhibitor or ARB treatment in line with NICE technology appraisals.

teach.h: Monitoring an ACE inhibitor or ARB
head: Result
Action
rows: 1–2 weeks after start or dose rise
eGFR fall under 25% / creatinine rise under 30%
No dose change; repeat in 1–2 weeks
Look for causes; stop or reduce
teach.caption: NICE NG203 recs 1.6.14–1.6.21. Volume depletion and NSAIDs are common causes of a fall in kidney function.

teach.text: A small creatinine rise after starting an ACE inhibitor is expected. Do not stop it if eGFR falls by less than 25% or creatinine rises by less than 30%: repeat in 1–2 weeks. And watch the numbers: 3 (A2 starts), 30 (A3 starts), 70 (tighter BP and referral threshold).

teach.h: Refer for specialist assessment if any (NG203 1.5.5)

children.label: eGFR down 25% + category change in 12 months
children.sub: Or down 15 or more a year

teach.h: Scenario: Mr Clarke in the practice clinic
teach.body: Mr Clarke, 70, has CKD G3b A2 and hypertension. He started ramipril 10 days ago. His eGFR has gone from 40 to 34 (a 15% fall) and potassium is 5.2. The nurse knows a fall under 25% means no dose change and a repeat test in 1–2 weeks. She checks he is not taking over-the-counter ibuprofen, gives dietary advice on potassium and salt, and books the repeat bloods.

items: CKD: eGFR below 60 and/or ACR 3+ for 3 months or more; classify by G and A.
BP: below 140/90 if ACR below 70; below 130/80 if ACR 70 or more.
Check potassium and eGFR before and 1–2 weeks after starting or increasing ACEi/ARB.
Stop RAS antagonist if potassium 6.0+; act if eGFR falls 25%+ or creatinine rises 30%+.
Refer: KFRE above 5%, ACR 70+, ACR above 30 with haematuria, rapid decline, resistant hypertension.

summary: You can now classify CKD by eGFR and ACR and set the NG203 blood pressure target. You can also monitor ACE inhibitors and ARBs safely and recognise the criteria for specialist referral.

A.q: Mrs Adeyemi, 66, has CKD with a urine ACR of 82 mg/mmol. What clinic blood pressure target does NICE NG203 set?
A.why: NICE NG203 rec 1.6.2: with ACR 70 mg/mmol or more, aim for clinic systolic below 130 (target 120–129) and diastolic below 80.

whyNot.0: Below 140/90 applies when ACR is below 70 mg/mmol.
whyNot.1: Below 150/90 is the NG136 clinic target for people aged 80 and over.
whyNot.3: NICE sets the systolic target range at 120–129, not below 120.

A.q: A man's eGFR is 52 mL/min/1.73 m² on a routine test. He has never been tested before. What should happen next?
A.why: NICE NG203 rec 1.1.8: confirm an eGFR below 60 in an adult not previously tested by repeating it within 2 weeks. CKD also needs 3 months' duration.

whyNot.0: One result is not enough; CKD needs confirmation and 3 months' duration.
whyNot.2: An eGFR of 52 alone does not meet referral criteria.
whyNot.3: 12 months is far too long to confirm a new low result.

A.q: Which urine test does NICE recommend for initial detection of proteinuria in adults?
A.why: NICE NG203 rec 1.1.12: use urine ACR rather than PCR because it is more sensitive for low levels of proteinuria.

whyNot.0: PCR is less sensitive than ACR for low-level proteinuria.
whyNot.1: Reagent strips should not be used to identify proteinuria in adults unless they detect albumin and are expressed as ACR.
whyNot.3: 24-hour collections are not the NG203 first-line test.

B.q: Mr Clarke started ramipril 10 days ago. His eGFR has fallen from 40 to 34 and potassium is 5.2 mmol/L. What does NICE advise?
options: No dose change; repeat in 1–2 weeks
B.why: NICE NG203 recs 1.6.19–1.6.20: do not modify the dose if eGFR falls by less than 25% (here 15%); repeat the test in 1–2 weeks.

whyNot.0: Stopping is considered if eGFR falls 25% or more or potassium reaches 6.0.
whyNot.1: NICE says do not combine renin–angiotensin antagonists.
whyNot.2: A dose reduction is not needed for a fall under 25%.

B.q: Before starting an ACE inhibitor, a woman with CKD has a potassium of 5.4 mmol/L. What does NICE NG203 say?
B.why: NICE NG203 rec 1.6.15: do not routinely offer a renin–angiotensin system antagonist if pretreatment potassium is greater than 5.0 mmol/L. Look for and treat other causes and recheck.

whyNot.0: Starting with potassium above 5.0 risks dangerous hyperkalaemia.
whyNot.1: Even if started, the recheck is due at 1–2 weeks, not 3 months.
whyNot.2: ARBs raise potassium in the same way.

B.q: Which result would prompt referral of an adult with CKD for specialist assessment?
B.why: NICE NG203 rec 1.5.5: refer if the 5-year risk of needing renal replacement therapy is greater than 5% (4-variable KFRE).

whyNot.1: ACR above 30 with haematuria, or 70 or more, are the protein triggers.
whyNot.2: A stable eGFR of 55 does not meet a decline criterion.
whyNot.3: Referral is for BP uncontrolled despite 4 antihypertensives.

C.q: Mr Hall, 58, has CKD and type 2 diabetes, eGFR 46 and ACR 12 mg/mmol. He is not yet on an ACE inhibitor or ARB. What does NICE recommend?
options: Offer an ACEi or ARB at the highest tolerated dose
Refer to nephrology before any treatment
Offer an ACEi and an ARB together
C.why: NICE NG203 rec 1.6.7: for adults with CKD and diabetes, offer an ARB or ACE inhibitor (titrated to the highest licensed dose tolerated) if ACR is 3 mg/mmol or more.

whyNot.1: ACR 70 is the threshold for people without diabetes; with diabetes it is 3.
whyNot.2: These results do not meet referral criteria; treatment starts in primary care.
whyNot.3: Combining renin–angiotensin antagonists is not recommended.

C.q: Mrs Ford has CKD and takes lisinopril. After a course of ibuprofen and a bout of diarrhoea, her creatinine has risen 40% from baseline. What should be done first?
options: Increase lisinopril to protect her kidneys
Look for causes such as dehydration and NSAIDs
Continue, as rises are expected on ACEi
C.why: NICE NG203 rec 1.6.21: if creatinine rises 30% or more, investigate other causes such as volume depletion or medicines (for example NSAIDs); if none is found, stop or reduce the RAS antagonist.

whyNot.0: Increasing the ACE inhibitor could worsen kidney function.
whyNot.2: A rise of 30% or more is beyond the expected change and needs action.
whyNot.3: Adding drugs before finding the cause misses reversible factors.

C.q: Mr Ito has CKD G4 and asks whether he should follow a very low-protein diet to protect his kidneys. What is the best response?
options: Yes, stop all dairy and meat
No; advice on potassium, salt, phosphate
C.why: NICE NG203 recs 1.4.7 and 1.4.9: do not offer low-protein diets (below 0.6–0.8 g/kg/day); offer dietary advice about potassium, phosphate, calorie and salt intake appropriate to severity.

whyNot.0: Low-protein diets are not offered to adults with CKD.
whyNot.1: Cutting out protein sources risks malnutrition and is not advised.
whyNot.3: High-protein intake is not recommended either; advice is individualised.

reteach.title: Two dials on the dashboard
reteach.question: Picture two dials: one shows filtering speed (eGFR), the other shows leak (ACR). What does each reading tell the nurse?

blocks.body: The filter dial (eGFR) gives the G stage: below 60 for 3 months is CKD. The leak dial (ACR) gives the A stage: 3 is the start of A2, 30 the start of A3, and 70 is the line for a tighter BP target (below 130/80) and referral if no diabetes explains it. The worse either dial, the higher the risk, and the more closely ACE inhibitors, ARBs and potassium are watched.

blocks.text: Potassium above 5.0: do not routinely start. Potassium 6.0 or more: stop.

explain.body: eGFR below 60 and/or ACR 3 or more for 3 months or more. G3a 45–59, G3b 30–44, G4 15–29, G5 below 15. A1 below 3, A2 3–30, A3 above 30 mg/mmol.

test.q: A woman has eGFR 38 and ACR 18 mg/mmol, both confirmed over 4 months. How is her CKD classified?
test.why: NICE NG203: eGFR 30–44 is G3b; ACR 3–30 is A2.

whyNot.0: G3a is 45–59 and A1 is below 3.

explain.body: ACR below 70: systolic below 140 (120–139), diastolic below 90. ACR 70 or more: systolic below 130 (120–129), diastolic below 80.

test.q: A man with CKD has an ACR of 40 mg/mmol. What is his clinic systolic target range?
test.why: NICE NG203 rec 1.6.1: with ACR under 70, aim for systolic below 140 (target range 120–139).

whyNot.0: This is below any NG203 range.
whyNot.1: 120–129 applies when ACR is 70 or more.

explain.body: Check potassium and eGFR before starting and 1–2 weeks after starting or each dose increase. Do not routinely start if potassium is above 5.0. Stop if it reaches 6.0 or more.

test.q: When should potassium and eGFR be rechecked after increasing the dose of an ARB in CKD?
test.why: NICE NG203 rec 1.6.14: repeat potassium and eGFR 1–2 weeks after starting and after each dose increase.

whyNot.1: 3 months is too long to detect hyperkalaemia.
whyNot.2: 24 hours is too early to see the effect.
whyNot.3: Annual review could miss dangerous hyperkalaemia.

explain.body: KFRE 5-year risk above 5%; ACR 70+ (unless diabetes and treated); ACR above 30 with haematuria; eGFR down 25% plus category change in 12 months, or 15+ a year; BP uncontrolled on 4 drugs; rare or genetic cause; renal artery stenosis.

test.q: A man's eGFR has fallen from 58 to 41 over 10 months. Does this meet NICE referral criteria?
options: No, the fall must be over 50%
Yes: sustained fall of 25%+ with category change
Yes, any fall in eGFR needs referral
test.why: NICE NG203 rec 1.5.5: refer for a sustained decrease in eGFR of 25% or more with a change in category within 12 months. 58 to 41 is a 29% fall, G3a to G3b.

whyNot.2: There is no eGFR-below-30 referral rule in NG203.
whyNot.3: Small changes are expected; NG203 sets specific thresholds.
